screens.title: Planning and Installation of Red Hat Satellite Server
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll walk through the planning, system preparation, installation, and initial steps required to get a Red Hat Satellite Server operational. You will learn how to evaluate capacity needs, prepare a RHEL host with subscriptions, DNS, NTP, and repositories, and how to execute the satellite-installer with the options that matter for provisioning and content sync. I’ll also highlight storage and network pitfalls that commonly derail deployments and describe the key post-installation tasks like importing your subscription manifest and triggering the first content sync. As an architect, you need to balance resources against growth: consider how many managed hosts you expect today and in the future, and plan storage and input and output accordingly. A brief example: a small lab might use 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of R A M, but production environments that manage thousands of hosts need far higher C P U, R A M, and most critically, fast storage under /var/lib/pulp. Finally, I’ll prompt you to check DNS and NTP early: incorrect FQDN or unsynchronized time commonly breaks certificate validation and service communication. Ready to explore the key topics and prepare a reliable Satellite installation?

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.2 › Practical Skills
Register and subscribe
sudo subscription-manager register --username=<YOUR_REDHAT_USERNAME> --password=<YOUR_REDHAT_PASSWORD> --auto-attach
sudo subscription-manager repos --enable=rhel-8-for-x86_64-baseos-rpms \
  --enable=rhel-8-for-x86_64-appstream-rpms \
  --enable=satellite-6.13-for-rhel-8-x86_64-rpms
Verify consumed subscriptions and enabled repos before installing packages needed by Satellite.
Host identity and time
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname satellite.lab.example.com
# If no DNS in lab
echo "192.168.122.10 satellite.lab.example.com satellite" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
sudo dnf install chrony -y
sudo systemctl enable --now chronyd
Confirm hostname resolution and chrony status; incorrect values lead to certificate and registration failures.
Installer checklist
  • Confirm FQDN resolves forward and reverse.
  • Ensure required ports will be open or that you understand the installer changes.
  • Decide on integrated vs external CA for production security.
Troubleshooting and logs
If installation fails, consult /var/log/foreman-installer/satellite.log for detailed errors. Common root causes are DNS, time skew, missing subscriptions, and insufficient disk I/O.

screens.title: Why planning and sizing matter
screens.narratorSegment: Planning and sizing are the foundation of a stable Satellite deployment. When we talk about sizing, we mean choosing C P U, R A M, and storage that match both current load and future growth. The most common mistakes come from underestimating storage and input and output. The directory /var/lib/pulp stores synchronized RPMs, metadata, and artifacts; as you add RHEL versions, architectures, and custom packages, that directory grows quickly and generates heavy read/write activity during syncs. For example, a lab with a few hundred hosts might be fine with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of R A M on SSD-backed storage, but an environment that will manage thousands of hosts typically requires many more vCPUs and 64 to 128 GB of R A M, plus RAID or SAN with high IOPS for /var/lib/pulp and a separate partition for /var/lib/pgsql. C P U and R A M affect concurrent tasks such as content synchronization, search indexing, and provisioning. Network bandwidth matters for pulling content from Red Hat CDN and distributing it to Capsules. A practical approach is to document expected managed hosts, expected content sets, and growth for 12–36 months, then map those to Red Hat's sizing guide. Misconception to avoid: adding more C P U or R A M cannot compensate for slow, undersized storage. The final takeaway: plan storage and input and output early, and separate critical data directories so you can scale them independently.

keyIdea.title: Sizing principle
keyIdea.text: Storage and I/O for /var/lib/pulp are the most commonly underestimated resource; plan and provision them first.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why planning and sizing matter

Sizing considerations

Map managed host counts and content volume to CPU, RAM, storage, and network. Prioritize fast storage for content, and separate the PostgreSQL database storage for independent scaling.

CPU & RAM: scale with concurrent tasks like syncs and provisioning.
Storage: /var/lib/pulp grows with products and architectures; use SSDs or high-IOPS SAN.
Network: ensure high-bandwidth, low-latency links to CDN and Capsules.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize fast, sized storage for /var/lib/pulp before scaling CPU or RAM; storage bottlenecks produce the largest operational impact.

Sizing scenario

Small lab
8 vCPUs, 32 GB RAM, single SSD, small product set
Production (thousands)
16+ vCPUs, 64–128 GB RAM, high-IOPS SAN, separate DB and pulp volumes
Common mistake
Relying on more CPU/RAM to fix slow syncs. If storage I/O is poor, performance won’t improve with CPU alone.

screens.title: Preparing the RHEL host
screens.narratorSegment: Preparing the host before running the installer is a sequence of essential steps that prevent many common failures. Start by registering the system with Red Hat and attaching the Satellite Infrastructure subscription; this provides access to the Satellite packages and associated repositories. Next, enable the required repositories for your RHEL major release; without correct repos the installer may fail to find packages. Set a fully qualified domain name and ensure it resolves both forward and reverse, because Satellite components and certificates rely on correct DNS. If you don't have a DNS server in your lab, add the host and its IP to /etc/hosts as a pragmatic workaround. Install and enable chronyd to ensure accurate time; certificate validation across services depends on synchronized time. Finally, review firewall expectations: the installer can manage firewall settings but you should understand which ports are required for services like HTTP, HTTPS, TFTP, Puppet, and Capsule communication. Concrete example commands include subscription-manager register and hostnamectl set-hostname, followed by enabling repos with subscription-manager repos. A common misconception is that the installer will magically fix DNS and time issues; it will not. Verify each prerequisite before invoking the installer to reduce install-time troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Host prep checklist
keyIdea.text: Register, enable repos, set resolvable FQDN, configure NTP, and confirm firewall requirements before installing.

content.html:
Process Flow › Preparing the RHEL host

Preparation steps

  1. Register with subscription-manager and attach the Satellite Infrastructure subscription.
  2. Enable RHEL base and Satellite repositories for your RHEL version.
  3. Set a resolvable FQDN; verify forward and reverse DNS.
  4. Install and enable chronyd for NTP synchronization.
  5. Understand and prepare firewall port requirements or allow the installer to configure them deliberately.
Pro Tip

If DNS is unavailable in a lab, add the FQDN and IP to /etc/hosts for predictable resolution during install.

Command examples

sudo subscription-manager register --username=<user> --password=<pass> --auto-attach
sudo subscription-manager repos --enable=rhel-8-for-x86_64-baseos-rpms \
  --enable=rhel-8-for-x86_64-appstream-rpms \
  --enable=satellite-6.13-for-rhel-8-x86_64-rpms
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname satellite.lab.example.com
sudo dnf install chrony -y
sudo systemctl enable --now chronyd
Verify subscription-manager list --consumed and hostname -f. Confirm chronyd is active to prevent certificate validation errors later.

screens.title: satellite-installer basics
screens.narratorSegment: The satellite-installer is the wrapper that runs Puppet modules to configure all Satellite components. You will typically invoke it with options that set the Foreman initial organization and location, admin credentials, and optional integrated services such as DNS, DHCP, and TFTP. A common installer invocation includes parameters to enable the foreman-proxy features that support provisioning. For example, enabling DNS and providing forwarders allows Satellite to become the authoritative resolver for provisioning networks. When you choose --certs-external-ca false, Satellite generates internal certificates suitable for lab or testing; for production, plan to integrate an external CA so certificates are trusted by your enterprise PKI. Installation can take tens of minutes to several hours depending on resource sizing and network speed. Watch the installer output for warnings and errors, and if something fails, consult /var/log/foreman-installer/satellite. log for detailed messages. One misconception is that the installer's default options suit every environment. Instead, review and specify the options you need for your network and provisioning model. The key takeaway: know the options you need, plan certificate handling, and be prepared to read logs to troubleshoot installation issues.

keyIdea.title: Installer guidance
keyIdea.text: Run satellite-installer with explicit options for organization, FQDN, and provisioning services; choose certificate strategy for lab vs production.

content.html:
Process › satellite-installer basics

Installer example

This example enables integrated DNS, DHCP, and TFTP for provisioning and uses internally generated certificates for a lab setup.

sudo satellite-installer \
--foreman-initial-organization "MyOrg" \
--foreman-initial-location "MyLocation" \
--foreman-admin-username "admin" \
--foreman-admin-password "StrongPassword123!" \
--foreman-proxy-dns true \
--foreman-proxy-dns-interface eth0 \
--foreman-proxy-dns-forwarders 8.8.8.8 \
--foreman-proxy-dhcp true \
--foreman-proxy-dhcp-interface eth0 \
--foreman-proxy-dhcp-range "192.168.100.10 192.168.100.200" \
--foreman-proxy-tftp true \
--foreman-proxy-tftp-interface eth0 \
--certs-external-ca false \
--certs-generate-apache-key true \
--enable-foreman-plugin-discovery \
--enable-foreman-plugin-bootdisk \
--enable-foreman-plugin-remote-execution
Monitor the installer output closely. If it stalls or exits with errors, check the detailed installer log at /var/log/foreman-installer/satellite.log.

Options explained

  • --foreman-admin-{username,password}: sets initial admin credentials.
  • --foreman-proxy-dns/dhcp/tftp: enable provisioning services on foreman-proxy.
  • --certs-external-ca: choose false for lab self-signed certs; use true when integrating an enterprise CA.
Common mistake

Assuming default installer options fit production networks; always review provisioning and certificate choices before running in production.

screens.title: FQDN and DNS requirements
screens.narratorSegment: A correct FQDN and reliable DNS are essential for Satellite to operate. Satellite components, certificates, and client registration rely on a resolvable hostname that maps cleanly to an IP address and back again. If forward or reverse DNS is missing or incorrect, services fail to start, certificate validation fails, and managed hosts cannot register. In a lab without an authoritative DNS server, adding an entry to /etc/hosts for the Satellite FQDN and IP is a sufficient workaround for testing, but this does not replace proper DNS in production. The installer will attempt to work with the host’s current hostname, but it will not repair incorrect DNS configurations. An example: if your Satellite is satellite. lab. example. com, ensure that host satellite. lab. example. com resolves to 192.168.122.10 and that a reverse lookup of 192.168.122.10 returns satellite. lab. example. com. Misconception to correct: people sometimes think they can use short hostnames; avoid them. Always use the full FQDN in certificate and provisioning contexts. Final takeaway: verify forward and reverse DNS before installing to avoid complicated troubleshooting later. FQDN and DNS requirements means forward and reverse dns entries for the satellite fqdn must be correct; use /etc/hosts only as a lab workaround.. In practical terms, why resolvable hostnames and reverse dns are critical. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › FQDN and DNS requirements

FQDN rules

  • Set a fully qualified domain name for the host used by Satellite.
  • Ensure forward lookup (name → IP) and reverse lookup (IP → name) are consistent.
  • Use the FQDN when specifying certificate common names and for client registration.
# Verify resolution
host satellite.lab.example.com
host 192.168.122.10

Lab workaround

If DNS is not available, add the FQDN and IP to /etc/hosts. This works for lab installs but is not suitable for production because many clients and services expect a DNS infrastructure.

Misconception

Short names or non-resolvable hostnames will break certificate issuance and host registration. Always use a fully qualified domain name.

screens.title: Certificate approaches
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a certificate strategy is an early design decision. For lab and testing environments, using the installer to generate internal, self-signed certificates is common and expedient. The option --certs-external-ca false instructs Satellite to create its own certificates. This reduces initial complexity but requires clients and administrators to trust those certificates manually. In production, integrating with an external Certificate Authority is recommended. An external CA provides certificates trusted by your enterprise PKI and simplifies trust for managed hosts and users, but it adds complexity during installation because you must prepare certificate signing requests and ensure all components accept the external CA. A practical example: labs often use generated certs for speed; production deployments use an enterprise CA to avoid manual trust steps across thousands of hosts. Misconception: a self-signed certificate is inherently insecure — it is secure for isolated labs if you accept the trust model, but it does not scale well to production. Final takeaway: plan certificate strategy early — use generated certs for labs, but integrate an external CA for production security and manageability. Certificate approaches means use generated certificates for labs; integrate an enterprise ca for production to ensure trust and manageability at scale.. In practical terms, self-signed internal certificates vs external ca integration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Certificates: internal vs external
Self-signed / generated (lab)
  • Quick to deploy with --certs-external-ca false.
  • Requires manual trust on clients or browser warnings.
  • Suitable for isolated test environments.
External CA (production)
  • Trusted by enterprise PKI and scales to many clients.
  • Requires CA integration steps before or during install.
  • Better operational security and fewer manual trust steps.
Key Takeaway

Pick external CA for production; generated certs are fine for labs but add trust overhead at scale.

screens.title: Post-installation tasks
screens.narratorSegment: After the installer completes, the installation is only the beginning. First, access the web UI at https://your_satellite_fqdn and log in with the admin credentials you set. Confirm core services are running and check the installer logs if any services fail. The next critical action is importing your Subscription Manifest from Red Hat. The manifest defines what content and subscriptions Satellite is entitled to and is required before you can synchronize Red Hat repositories. After importing the manifest, create Products and Repositories for the RHEL versions you will manage and initiate the first synchronization. This initial sync can be large and will exercise storage and network; monitor disk usage under /var/lib/pulp and watch for input and output saturation. Decide whether you will use katello-agent or foreman-client for client tasks; foreman-client is preferred for newer deployments. A common mistake is skipping the manifest import and attempting to sync; without the manifest, synchronizations will fail. Final question to consider: have you confirmed that your storage and network can handle the initial sync workload? Post-installation tasks means import the subscription manifest, then create products and repositories and run the first content sync while monitoring storage and i/o.. In practical terms, validate services, import manifest, and start first content sync. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

First checklist

Navigate to Content › Subscriptions › Manage Manifest to upload the manifest you downloaded from your Red Hat account. Without this manifest, product synchronization will be blocked.

screens.title: Subscription manifest and content sync
screens.narratorSegment: The subscription manifest is a file you download from your Red Hat account that declares entitlement to content and subscriptions. Uploading it into Satellite is mandatory for accessing Red Hat content through Satellite. The manifest ties your organization to specific repository entitlements and allows Satellite to list and synchronize those repositories. After you upload the manifest, you create Products mapped to supported RHEL versions and add the repositories you need. When you initiate synchronization, Satellite pulls content from the Red Hat CDN into /var/lib/pulp. That operation uses significant network and disk resources and can take a long time on poorly sized systems. An illustrative example: after importing a manifest and selecting the BaseOS and AppStream repositories for RHEL 8, the initial sync retrieves all RPMs and metadata for those repositories. A common misconception is that uploading the manifest automatically performs syncs; you must explicitly create products and trigger repository syncs. Final thought: treat the manifest upload as the gate that unlocks content management in Satellite; plan bandwidth and storage accordingly before syncing. Definition › Subscription manifest & sync

What the manifest does

The manifest contains your entitlement information. After upload, Satellite can list the repositories you may sync and distribute to managed hosts.

Step: Content › Subscriptions › Manage Manifest — upload the manifest file obtained from Red Hat.
Common mistake

Uploading a manifest does not automatically sync repositories; you must create products and initiate repository syncs.

Sync example

screens.title: Separating data volumes
screens.narratorSegment: Separating data volumes for content and the database improves performance and scalability. The Pulp content store under /var/lib/pulp is where RPMs, metadata, and kickstart artifacts live. PostgreSQL stores metadata and transactional data under /var/lib/pgsql. Placing pulp and PostgreSQL on different disks or partitions reduces input and output contention: heavy content synchronization generates large reads and writes that can starve database input and output if both share the same volume. In production, give pulp the fastest storage available because large sequential and random input and output patterns occur during syncs and content serving. PostgreSQL benefits from reliable low-latency IOPS and dedicated backups. A common deployment pattern is to use SSDs or high-performance SAN for /var/lib/pulp and a separate mirrored or clustered solution for /var/lib/pgsql. Misconception: a single large disk is simpler; but it creates a single point of input and output contention and complicates recovery. Final takeaway: design storage with separate volumes and growth plans for both pulp and PostgreSQL, and ensure your backup strategy covers both independently. Separating data volumes means keep /var/lib/pulp and /var/lib/pgsql on separate, appropriately sized volumes to avoid i/o contention and to enable independent scaling and backup.. In practical terms, why /var/lib/pulp and /var/lib/pgsql should be on distinct volumes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Storage architecture
keyIdea.text: Keep /var/lib/pulp and /var/lib/pgsql on separate, appropriately sized volumes to avoid I/O contention and to enable independent scaling and backup.

content.html:
Architecture › Separate data volumes

Why separate volumes?

Separation prevents Pulp sync I/O from impacting PostgreSQL performance and allows independent scaling and backups.

/var/lib/pulp — stores RPMs, metadata, and artifacts. Requires high throughput and capacity.
/var/lib/pgsql — stores the database. Requires low latency and reliable IOPS.

Deployment pattern

Use SSD or high-IOPS SAN for pulp. Use RAID or dedicated database storage for PostgreSQL, and plan backups and retention independently. Scaling one does not force changing the other when separated.
Misconception

A single large disk is easier but creates performance contention and complicates growth planning and disaster recovery.

screens.title: Firewall and ports
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding firewall requirements prevents post-install communication issues. Satellite and its services use multiple ports: HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443) for web access; ports for puppet, proxy, and capsules; TFTP and DHCP for network boot and provisioning; and additional ports for remote execution and service APIs. The satellite-installer can configure firewall rules when requested, but administrators should still audit and approve these changes. If you use integrated TFTP and DHCP for provisioning, ensure those ports are open and that DHCP ranges do not conflict with existing DHCP servers on the network. For environments with strict change control, pre-open firewall ports or coordinate with the networking team before running the installer. A practical checklist includes verifying that 80 and 443 are available, confirming TFTP and DHCP settings for provisioning interfaces, and ensuring capsule-to-satellite connectivity ports are reachable. Misconception: leaving firewall closed and expecting the installer to succeed—this often leads to service start failures and requires manual correction. Final question: have you documented required ports and obtained change control approval where necessary? Firewall and ports means validate required ports for web ui, provisioning, and capsule communication before or during installation to avoid blocked services.. In practical terms, ports commonly required by satellite and provisioning services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Firewall and ports

Common ports

  • 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS) — web UI and API.
  • 8140 — Puppet agent/master communication.
  • 5647, 9090 — ancillary service ports used by Satellite components.
  • 69 (TFTP), 67/68 (DHCP) — provisioning services if enabled.
Coordinate DHCP and TFTP enablement carefully to avoid network conflicts with existing infrastructure.

Checklist

Document the ports, request network changes as needed, and confirm that the provisioning interface has the expected routing and DHCP behavior.
Common mistake

Assuming the installer will fully correct firewall issues. It may configure rules, but missing network approvals or conflicting services still block proper operation.

screens.title: Common installation pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Several pitfalls recur in Satellite installations. First, incorrect FQDN or missing reverse DNS will cause component failures and certificate problems. Second, missing or incorrect subscriptions prevent access to required repositories and will block package installation and content syncs. Third, insufficient or slow storage for /var/lib/pulp leads to long sync times, failed tasks, and a sluggish UI. Fourth, firewall misconfiguration or conflicting DHCP servers will break provisioning. Finally, ignoring logs is a mistake: the installer outputs detailed information and writes logs to /var/log/foreman-installer/satellite. log which often point directly to the root cause. The practical strategy is to validate prerequisites one by one: confirm subscription-manager output, verify hostname -f and host lookups, enable the correct repos and run a small package install to test, check chronyd status, and confirm disk space with df -h and input and output health with iostat. If you plan a production install, create a rollback or snapshot before major changes. Misconception: guessing resource needs or skipping prechecks; thorough verification before install reduces failure frequency and simplifies troubleshooting. Final reflective question: which prerequisite would you validate first and why?

Common Pitfalls › Installation pitfalls

Checklist to prevent failures

  • Confirm subscription-manager shows the Satellite Infrastructure entitlement.
  • Check disk space and I/O performance for /var/lib/pulp.
  • Review firewall rules and DHCP/TFTP responsibilities on the network.

hostname -f
sudo subscription-manager list --consumed
df -h /var/lib/pulp
sudo systemctl status chronyd
Key Takeaway

Run a short verification script of host identity, subscriptions, time sync, and storage before running the installer.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll walk through the planning, system preparation, installation, and initial steps required to get a Red Hat Satellite Server operational. You will learn how to evaluate capacity needs, prepare a RHEL host with subscriptions, DNS, NTP, and repositories, and how to execute the satellite-installer with the options that matter for provisioning and content sync. I’ll also highlight storage and network pitfalls that commonly derail deployments and describe the key post-installation tasks like importing your subscription manifest and triggering the first content sync. As an architect, you need to balance resources against growth: consider how many managed hosts you expect today and in the future, and plan storage and input and output accordingly. A brief example: a small lab might use 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of R A M, but production environments that manage thousands of hosts need far higher C P U, R A M, and most critically, fast storage under /var/lib/pulp. Finally, I’ll prompt you to check DNS and NTP early: incorrect FQDN or unsynchronized time commonly breaks certificate validation and service communication. Ready to explore the key topics and prepare a reliable Satellite installation?

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to identify prerequisites and size resources for Satellite, prepare a RHEL host for installation, run the satellite-installer with appropriate options, and perform the necessary post-installation tasks to make Satellite functional. First, sizing: you will learn to translate managed-host counts into C P U, R A M, and storage requirements and understand why fast storage for /var/lib/pulp is critical. Second, host preparation: you will practice registering a system, enabling required repositories, setting an FQDN and DNS, and ensuring NTP and firewall readiness. Third, installation: you will gain familiarity with satellite-installer options used to define FQDN, organization, DNS/DHCP/TFTP settings, and certificate choices. Fourth, post-install: you will validate the web UI, import your subscription manifest, start the first content synchronization, and choose a client registration method. Each objective includes a short practical milestone so you can verify competency in a lab. Keep these goals in mind as we work from planning to a functioning Satellite server.

This second objectives screen turns goals into practical skills: registering systems and managing repositories, verifying DNS and time, running the installer with options, and troubleshooting common failures. You will practise the subscription-manager commands to register and attach subscriptions, enable the satellite repositories needed for installation, and update the system packages. You will configure a resolvable FQDN and, if DNS is not available in your lab, add an /etc/hosts entry to mirror production behavior. For time sync you will install and enable chronyd and confirm the service status. When executing satellite-installer, you will specify organization and location, choose whether to enable integrated DNS/DHCP/TFTP, and decide on internal or external certificate authorities. Finally, you will learn to read installer logs and where to find detailed error output. Each objective ends with a small verification step so you can mark the skill as complete in your lab checklist.

Planning and sizing are the foundation of a stable Satellite deployment. When we talk about sizing, we mean choosing C P U, R A M, and storage that match both current load and future growth. The most common mistakes come from underestimating storage and input and output. The directory /var/lib/pulp stores synchronized RPMs, metadata, and artifacts; as you add RHEL versions, architectures, and custom packages, that directory grows quickly and generates heavy read/write activity during syncs. For example, a lab with a few hundred hosts might be fine with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB of R A M on SSD-backed storage, but an environment that will manage thousands of hosts typically requires many more vCPUs and 64 to 128 GB of R A M, plus RAID or SAN with high IOPS for /var/lib/pulp and a separate partition for /var/lib/pgsql. C P U and R A M affect concurrent tasks such as content synchronization, search indexing, and provisioning. Network bandwidth matters for pulling content from Red Hat CDN and distributing it to Capsules. A practical approach is to document expected managed hosts, expected content sets, and growth for 12–36 months, then map those to Red Hat's sizing guide. Misconception to avoid: adding more C P U or R A M cannot compensate for slow, undersized storage. The final takeaway: plan storage and input and output early, and separate critical data directories so you can scale them independently.

Preparing the host before running the installer is a sequence of essential steps that prevent many common failures. Start by registering the system with Red Hat and attaching the Satellite Infrastructure subscription; this provides access to the Satellite packages and associated repositories. Next, enable the required repositories for your RHEL major release; without correct repos the installer may fail to find packages. Set a fully qualified domain name and ensure it resolves both forward and reverse, because Satellite components and certificates rely on correct DNS. If you don't have a DNS server in your lab, add the host and its IP to /etc/hosts as a pragmatic workaround. Install and enable chronyd to ensure accurate time; certificate validation across services depends on synchronized time. Finally, review firewall expectations: the installer can manage firewall settings but you should understand which ports are required for services like HTTP, HTTPS, TFTP, Puppet, and Capsule communication. Concrete example commands include subscription-manager register and hostnamectl set-hostname, followed by enabling repos with subscription-manager repos. A common misconception is that the installer will magically fix DNS and time issues; it will not. Verify each prerequisite before invoking the installer to reduce install-time troubleshooting.

The satellite-installer is the wrapper that runs Puppet modules to configure all Satellite components. You will typically invoke it with options that set the Foreman initial organization and location, admin credentials, and optional integrated services such as DNS, DHCP, and TFTP. A common installer invocation includes parameters to enable the foreman-proxy features that support provisioning. For example, enabling DNS and providing forwarders allows Satellite to become the authoritative resolver for provisioning networks. When you choose --certs-external-ca false, Satellite generates internal certificates suitable for lab or testing; for production, plan to integrate an external CA so certificates are trusted by your enterprise PKI. Installation can take tens of minutes to several hours depending on resource sizing and network speed. Watch the installer output for warnings and errors, and if something fails, consult /var/log/foreman-installer/satellite. log for detailed messages. One misconception is that the installer's default options suit every environment. Instead, review and specify the options you need for your network and provisioning model. The key takeaway: know the options you need, plan certificate handling, and be prepared to read logs to troubleshoot installation issues.

A correct FQDN and reliable DNS are essential for Satellite to operate. Satellite components, certificates, and client registration rely on a resolvable hostname that maps cleanly to an IP address and back again. If forward or reverse DNS is missing or incorrect, services fail to start, certificate validation fails, and managed hosts cannot register. In a lab without an authoritative DNS server, adding an entry to /etc/hosts for the Satellite FQDN and IP is a sufficient workaround for testing, but this does not replace proper DNS in production. The installer will attempt to work with the host’s current hostname, but it will not repair incorrect DNS configurations. An example: if your Satellite is satellite. lab. example. com, ensure that host satellite. lab. example. com resolves to 192.168.122.10 and that a reverse lookup of 192.168.122.10 returns satellite. lab. example. com. Misconception to correct: people sometimes think they can use short hostnames; avoid them. Always use the full FQDN in certificate and provisioning contexts. Final takeaway: verify forward and reverse DNS before installing to avoid complicated troubleshooting later. FQDN and DNS requirements means forward and reverse dns entries for the satellite fqdn must be correct; use /etc/hosts only as a lab workaround.. In practical terms, why resolvable hostnames and reverse dns are critical. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing a certificate strategy is an early design decision. For lab and testing environments, using the installer to generate internal, self-signed certificates is common and expedient. The option --certs-external-ca false instructs Satellite to create its own certificates. This reduces initial complexity but requires clients and administrators to trust those certificates manually. In production, integrating with an external Certificate Authority is recommended. An external CA provides certificates trusted by your enterprise PKI and simplifies trust for managed hosts and users, but it adds complexity during installation because you must prepare certificate signing requests and ensure all components accept the external CA. A practical example: labs often use generated certs for speed; production deployments use an enterprise CA to avoid manual trust steps across thousands of hosts. Misconception: a self-signed certificate is inherently insecure — it is secure for isolated labs if you accept the trust model, but it does not scale well to production. Final takeaway: plan certificate strategy early — use generated certs for labs, but integrate an external CA for production security and manageability. Separating data volumes for content and the database improves performance and scalability. The Pulp content store under /var/lib/pulp is where RPMs, metadata, and kickstart artifacts live. PostgreSQL stores metadata and transactional data under /var/lib/pgsql. Placing pulp and PostgreSQL on different disks or partitions reduces input and output contention: heavy content synchronization generates large reads and writes that can starve database input and output if both share the same volume. In production, give pulp the fastest storage available because large sequential and random input and output patterns occur during syncs and content serving. PostgreSQL benefits from reliable low-latency IOPS and dedicated backups. A common deployment pattern is to use SSDs or high-performance SAN for /var/lib/pulp and a separate mirrored or clustered solution for /var/lib/pgsql. Misconception: a single large disk is simpler; but it creates a single point of input and output contention and complicates recovery. Final takeaway: design storage with separate volumes and growth plans for both pulp and PostgreSQL, and ensure your backup strategy covers both independently. Several pitfalls recur in Satellite installations. First, incorrect FQDN or missing reverse DNS will cause component failures and certificate problems. Second, missing or incorrect subscriptions prevent access to required repositories and will block package installation and content syncs. Third, insufficient or slow storage for /var/lib/pulp leads to long sync times, failed tasks, and a sluggish UI. Fourth, firewall misconfiguration or conflicting DHCP servers will break provisioning. Finally, ignoring logs is a mistake: the installer outputs detailed information and writes logs to /var/log/foreman-installer/satellite. log which often point directly to the root cause. The practical strategy is to validate prerequisites one by one: confirm subscription-manager output, verify hostname -f and host lookups, enable the correct repos and run a small package install to test, check chronyd status, and confirm disk space with df -h and input and output health with iostat. If you plan a production install, create a rollback or snapshot before major changes. Misconception: guessing resource needs or skipping prechecks; thorough verification before install reduces failure frequency and simplifies troubleshooting.
